live.name: BRONZE SATIN
live.headline: BRONZE SATIN: what the catalogue records about this tracked threat actor
live.in_short: BRONZE SATIN is Secureworks' name for an actor also tracked as HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon. The catalogue lists two web shell tools. No report card gives more detail.

sentences.t: BRONZE SATIN is the name used in the Secureworks entry for this threat actor.
The catalogue lists three other names for the same actor: HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
The catalogue lists two tools for this actor: ChinaChopper and Godzilla Webshell.

next.headline: BRONZE SATIN: the espionage group also tracked as HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon
next.in_short: Secureworks tracks BRONZE SATIN, also called HAFNIUM and Silk Typhoon. Governments and vendors tie it to the 2021 Exchange attacks, and one outlet reports a link to a US Treasury breach. Several links rest on named sources.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as BRONZE SATIN. Other names for it are HAFNIUM, Murky Panda and Silk Typhoon.
BleepingComputer describes Silk Typhoon, also known as Hafnium, as a Chinese nation-state hacking group.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre assessed it was highly likely that HAFNIUM, which it associates with the Chinese state, was responsible for the early-2021 Exchange server intrusions.

In December 2022 the US and allies attributed the Exchange campaign to hackers affiliated with China's Ministry of State Security. Microsoft had earlier assessed with high confidence that HAFNIUM was exploiting the flaws.

BleepingComputer says the group has targeted organisations in the United States, Australia, Japan and Vietnam. These include defense contractors, policy think tanks, NGOs, healthcare, law firms and universities.

Italian media (ANSA), as relayed by BleepingComputer, link Silk Typhoon to 2020 attacks on infectious disease researchers and healthcare bodies seeking COVID vaccine data. The report does not confirm this itself.
The Secureworks catalogue record lists two web shells among the group's tools: ChinaChopper and Godzilla Webshell.
A Wikipedia article on China Chopper says Hafnium used a JScript version of it in 2021 to exploit four zero-day flaws in Microsoft Exchange Server.
Elastic saw web shells, credential harvesting, mailbox theft and new accounts after Exchange exploitation. It said the activity resembled HAFNIUM but could be other, opportunistic threats.
BleepingComputer says the group's espionage mainly focuses on data theft and reconnaissance.
BleepingComputer reports that Microsoft said in March 2025 that Silk Typhoon had begun targeting remote management tools and cloud services in supply chains.
Kaspersky says Microsoft reported on March 2, 2021 that HAFNIUM was exploiting four zero-days in Exchange.
The NCSC cites open-source reporting that at least 30,000 organisations were compromised in the US alone. A senior US official later said the campaign hit hundreds of thousands of systems worldwide.

BleepingComputer, citing Bloomberg and two people familiar with the matter, links Silk Typhoon to a hack of the US Treasury's OFAC in early December. Attackers used a stolen API key to get into a BeyondTrust instance.

Italian police arrested Xu Zewei at Milan's Malpensa Airport on July 3 on a US warrant. Italian media (ANSA) say Xu is accused of links to Silk Typhoon. The US is seeking extradition, and no decision is reported.
Patch internet-facing servers quickly, check them for web shells, and watch how remote management tools and their keys are used.
